name: Pattern Completion
blurb: A piece is missing from the pattern. Which piece fits?
childIntro: Part of this pattern has been cut out. Look at the pattern all around the hole. Which piece belongs there?
howItWorks: Pearson describes this as perceiving a pattern within a large shape where a piece is missing, then extending the pattern into that space. It is the easiest of the four NNAT question types and it appears at every level from kindergarten upwards. There are always five answers to choose from, and the missing piece is marked with a dashed box.
parentTip: This one rewards looking around the hole rather than at it. Get your child to read the row the hole is in, left to right, and then the column it is in, top to bottom. The answer has to satisfy both. Remember the NNAT uses only black, white, yellow, blue and green, and it is checked so that color-blind children are not disadvantaged.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: A pattern of yellow and blue squares with one square missing.

questions.explanation: The colors take turns: yellow, blue, yellow on the top row, then blue, yellow on the bottom. The next one after yellow is blue.
questions.strategy: Read the pattern out loud like a chant. Yellow, blue, yellow, blue. What comes next?

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid of circles. Each row is one color. One circle is missing from the bottom row.

questions.explanation: Every circle in a row is the same color. The bottom row is green, so the missing circle is green. Choice d is green but it is a square, and every other piece is a circle.
questions.strategy: Check the row the hole is in. All the other pieces in that row tell you the answer.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid of triangles. Each column is one color. One triangle is missing.

questions.explanation: This time the color follows the column, not the row. The middle column is green above the hole, so the missing piece is green and points up like all the others. Choice d is green but upside down.
questions.strategy: If reading across does not work, read up and down instead.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: A checkerboard of blue and yellow squares with one square missing.

questions.explanation: The colors alternate like a chessboard. Every square touching the hole from the side is blue, so the hole itself must be yellow. Check it both ways: the row goes blue, yellow, blue, and the column goes yellow, blue, yellow.
questions.strategy: On a checkerboard, look at the square directly above the hole. The answer is always the other color.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: A repeating pattern of circle, square, circle, square with one piece missing.

questions.explanation: Two rules are running at once. The shape goes circle, square, circle, square along each row. The color is set by the row: blue on top, yellow underneath. The hole is in a circle position on the yellow row, so it is a yellow circle.
questions.strategy: One rule for the shape and one for the color. Work them out separately, then put them together.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid where each row has the same shape and each column has the same color.

questions.explanation: The row decides the shape and the column decides the color. The hole is in the circle row and the blue column, so it is a blue circle. Choice b has the right color but the wrong shape.
questions.strategy: Point at the row, say the shape. Point at the column, say the color. Put them together.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid of arrows all pointing in a turning pattern, with one missing.

questions.explanation: Each arrow turns a quarter turn clockwise as you move right, and again as you move down. Following the bottom row from the left, the arrows go down then left, so the next one points up again after a full turn: it points right, back where the pattern started.
questions.strategy: Follow just one arrow tip around the grid. It is easier than watching the whole arrow.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid where the number of dots increases across each row.

questions.explanation: Every row counts one, two, three. The hole is in the third position, so it holds three dots. Choice c has four, which is one too many.
questions.strategy: Count each row before you guess. The pattern repeats from row to row.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid where shapes are solid on the outside and outlined in the middle, with one missing.

questions.explanation: Two patterns overlap. The color is fixed by the row: blue, yellow, green. The fill alternates solid and empty across each row. The bottom row goes solid, empty, so the next is solid, and the color is green.
questions.strategy: When two rules overlap, write them out separately. Color from the row, fill from the position.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: A repeating pattern of three shapes with one missing.

questions.explanation: The pattern is triangle, square, circle, over and over, running left to right and carrying on from the end of the top row to the start of the bottom row. Counting along, the hole falls on a triangle. Choice e is a triangle but upside down, and no shape in the pattern is upside down.
questions.strategy: When a pattern of three does not line up with the columns, count all the way along from the very first shape.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A grid of squares in a repeating three-color pattern with one missing.

questions.explanation: The three colors repeat in the same order everywhere: blue, yellow, green. The square to the left of the hole is blue and the one to the right is green, so the hole is yellow.
questions.strategy: The two squares either side of a hole are often enough on their own. Check them first.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A grid where each shape has a different number of sides, growing across each row.

questions.explanation: Across each row the number of sides climbs: three, four, five. Down each column the color changes: green, blue, yellow. The hole is in the four-sided position on the yellow row, so it is a yellow square.
questions.strategy: Count sides rather than naming shapes. Three, four, five is a clearer pattern than triangle, square, pentagon.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A grid of shapes that get larger across each row.

questions.explanation: Shapes grow from small to medium to large across every row. The row decides the shape. The bottom row is triangles, and the hole is in the large position, so it is a large blue triangle.
questions.strategy: Size is a pattern just like color. Small, medium, large is a three-step sequence.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A grid where each shape has a small dot in a different corner, moving around.

questions.explanation: In every row the dot starts at the top left, moves to the top right, then drops to the bottom right. The bottom row is blue and the dot has reached the top right, so next it goes to the bottom right. Choice b puts it in the bottom left corner, which never happens.
questions.strategy: Track the small detail, not the big shape. The dot is doing all the work here.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A grid where two things change at once: shape count and fill.

questions.explanation: Three rules run together. The row fixes the shape and its color. The count goes one, two, three across. The fill goes solid, empty, solid. The hole needs three solid green squares. Choice b keeps the empty fill from the middle column.
questions.strategy: Three rules means three checks. Shape and color, then count, then fill. Do not stop after two.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A checkerboard of green and yellow with one square missing.

questions.explanation: Colors alternate along every row and down every column. The squares on both sides of the hole are yellow, and the square directly above it is yellow, so the hole must be green.
questions.strategy: Check the neighbor above and the neighbor beside. Both must disagree with your answer on a checkerboard.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A grid of shapes rotating steadily across and down.

questions.explanation: Every step to the right turns the shape by an eighth of a full turn, and so does every step down. The bottom row runs ninety, one hundred and thirty-five, so the next is one hundred and eighty.
questions.strategy: Work out the size of one step, then just add it on. Do not try to see the whole rotation at once.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A grid where the number of shapes decreases across each row.

questions.explanation: The count drops by two across each row: five, three, one. The color comes from the row. So the hole holds one green diamond. Choice b has two, which does not fit the drop of two.
questions.strategy: Falling patterns are as common as rising ones. Say the numbers backwards to check: five, three, one.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A grid where a large shape holds a smaller shape inside, changing across the rows.

questions.explanation: The outer shape belongs to the row and the inner shape belongs to the column. The bottom row uses hexagons and the last column uses stars, so the hole is a hexagon with a star inside.
questions.strategy: When shapes are nested, treat the outside and the inside as two separate patterns.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A long repeating pattern of four shapes with one missing near the end.

questions.explanation: A group of three repeats endlessly: blue circle, yellow square, green triangle. Because the grid is four wide and the group is three long, the pattern does not line up with the columns. Count straight along from the start and the hole lands on a yellow square. Choice d has the right shape but the wrong color, and choice e is tilted when nothing in the pattern is tilted.
questions.strategy: When the repeat length and the row length do not match, ignore the rows. Read the whole grid as one long line.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: Green triangles and green hexagons taking turns in two rows. The last piece is missing.

questions.explanation: The shapes take turns all the way along: triangle, hexagon, triangle, hexagon. The piece just before the hole is a triangle, so the hole is a hexagon. The green triangle is wrong because it would put two triangles side by side.
questions.strategy: Say the pattern out loud as you point at it: triangle, hexagon, triangle, hexagon.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: Diamonds taking turns: a filled blue one, then an empty gray one. The last diamond is missing.

questions.explanation: The diamonds take turns: filled blue, empty gray, filled blue, empty gray. The one just before the hole is filled blue, so the hole is an empty gray diamond. The filled gray diamond is gray but it is filled in, and every second diamond is empty.
questions.strategy: Look at the piece right before the hole. In a taking-turns pattern it tells you the answer.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid of blue shapes. Each row has its own shape. One shape in the bottom row is missing.

questions.explanation: Every shape in a row is the same, and the bottom row is stars, so the hole is a star. The yellow star is wrong because nothing in this grid is yellow. Blue never changes anywhere.
questions.strategy: Notice what stays the same as well as what changes. Here the color never changes at all.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: Two rows of squares. Each column has its own color and its own pattern inside. One square is missing.

questions.explanation: Read up and down instead of across. The square above the hole is green with dots, so the hole is green with dots too. The filled green square has the right color but no dots, and every square in that column has dots.
questions.strategy: When across does not work, look straight up. The piece above the hole is often the whole answer.

questions.prompt: Which piece belongs in the empty space?

figure.alt: Green circles and gray squares in a checkerboard. The middle piece is missing.

questions.explanation: Green circles and gray squares take turns going across and going down. Every piece touching the hole is a gray square, so the hole has to be a green circle. The green square is the right color but the wrong shape.
questions.strategy: Look at the piece above the hole and the piece beside it. In a checkerboard they are both the other kind.

questions.prompt: Which piece belongs in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid where each column has its own shape and each row has its own color. One piece is missing.

questions.explanation: Two things are going on. The shape comes from the column, which is the six-pointed star, and the color comes from the row, which is green. The blue star has the right shape but the color belongs to the middle row.
questions.strategy: Check the column first, then the row. The answer must match both.

questions.prompt: Which piece belongs in the empty space?

figure.alt: Two rows of ovals. The top row is blue and the bottom row is green. Filled and empty ovals take turns. One oval is missing.

questions.explanation: The color comes from the row, so the hole is green. Filled and empty take turns along the row, and the oval before the hole is empty, so the hole is filled. The empty green oval breaks the taking-turns rule and would put two empty ovals side by side.
questions.strategy: Work out the two rules one at a time. First the color, then filled or empty.

questions.prompt: Which piece belongs in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid of blue dots. The number of dots grows by one going across and by one going down. The last box is missing.

questions.explanation: One more dot appears each step to the right, and one more each step down. The bottom row runs three, four, so the hole holds five. Four is the box to the left of the hole, not the hole itself.
questions.strategy: Count the boxes on either side of the hole and work out the size of one step.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: Eight squares in two rows. They keep repeating: filled blue, striped yellow, empty green. One square is missing.

questions.explanation: Three squares keep repeating in the same order: filled blue, striped yellow, empty green. The pattern does not stop at the end of the top row, it carries straight on to the bottom row. The square before the hole is striped yellow, so the hole is an empty green square, not the filled green one.
questions.strategy: Read the whole grid as one long line: top row first, then keep going on the bottom row.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: Six empty gray squares. Each one holds a small black dot, and the dot sits where that square sits in the grid. One square is missing.

choices.label: an empty gray square with a black dot near the bottom middle
an empty gray square with a black dot near the top middle
an empty gray square with a black dot near the bottom left
an empty gray square with a black dot right in the middle
an empty yellow square with a black dot near the bottom middle

questions.explanation: The little dot copies where its own square sits. The hole is in the bottom row and the middle column, so its dot goes low down and in the middle. The one with the dot near the top middle has the right column but the wrong row.
questions.strategy: Ignore the big shape and watch the small dot. The dot is doing all the work.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: Green triangles pointing up and yellow triangles pointing down, taking turns. The last one is missing.

choices.label: an empty yellow triangle pointing down

questions.explanation: Up and down take turns all the way along, and the color turns with them. The piece before the hole points up, so the hole points down and is yellow. The yellow triangle pointing up has the right color but faces the wrong way.
questions.strategy: Two clues move together here. Check the way it points as well as the color.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid where every piece in a row is the same shape and the same color. One piece in the top row is missing.

questions.explanation: Everything in a row matches, and the top row is gray crosses. So the hole is a gray cross. The blue cross has the right shape but blue belongs to the middle row.
questions.strategy: Read the row the hole is in. Everything else in that row is the answer.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: Two rows of gray shapes repeating in the same order. One shape is missing.

choices.label: a gray bowtie standing on end

questions.explanation: Four shapes repeat in the same order, and the piece straight above the hole is a bowtie. So the hole is a bowtie too. The blue bowtie is the right shape, but every single piece here is gray.
questions.strategy: When a grid repeats, the piece directly above the hole is usually the same as the hole.

questions.prompt: Which piece belongs in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid of pentagons. Each column has its own color and its own filling. One pentagon is missing.

choices.label: a green pentagon with flat stripes
a blue pentagon with flat stripes
a green hexagon with flat stripes

questions.explanation: Every pentagon in a column is colored and filled the same way. The middle column is green with stripes, so the hole is green with stripes. The filled green pentagon is the right color but it has lost its stripes.
questions.strategy: Two clues travel together down a column. Match both before you choose.

questions.prompt: Which piece belongs in the empty space?

figure.alt: A big checkerboard of blue squares and yellow circles with one piece missing.

questions.explanation: Blue squares and yellow circles take turns in every direction. The pieces above, below and beside the hole are all blue squares, so the hole is a yellow circle. The yellow square mixes up the two pieces: yellow always goes with a circle here.
questions.strategy: In a checkerboard, the answer is always the opposite of its neighbors.

questions.prompt: Which piece belongs in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid of octagons. The filling comes from the column and the color comes from the row. One octagon is missing.

choices.label: a green octagon with slanted stripes
a yellow octagon with slanted stripes
a green hexagon with slanted stripes

questions.explanation: Look up the column for the filling and along the row for the color. The middle column is striped and the bottom row is green, so the hole is a green striped octagon. The filled green octagon got the color right and forgot the stripes.
questions.strategy: Say the two rules out loud before looking at the answers: stripes from the column, color from the row.

questions.prompt: Which piece belongs in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid of four-pointed stars. Each row is one color, and filled and dotted stars take turns along every row. One star is missing.

choices.label: a blue star with upright stripes
a blue six-pointed star with dots

questions.explanation: The color comes from the row, so the hole is blue. Along the row, filled and dotted take turns, and the star before the hole is filled, so the hole has dots. The filled blue star gets the color right but breaks the taking-turns rule.
questions.strategy: Do one rule at a time. Get the color from the row, then get the filling from its neighbor.

questions.prompt: Which piece belongs in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid of green half circles. The number jumps by two going across and by one going down. The last box is missing.

questions.explanation: Each step to the right adds two, so the bottom row goes three, five, seven. Six is what you get if you add only one, which is the down jump, not the across jump. The hole holds seven half circles.
questions.strategy: Work out the size of the across jump and the down jump separately. They are not always the same.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: Twelve hexagons that keep repeating: filled blue, dotted yellow, empty green. One hexagon is missing.

questions.explanation: Three hexagons repeat over and over, but the rows are four wide, so the pattern does not line up underneath itself. Read it as one long line and the piece before the hole is filled blue, so the hole is dotted yellow. The empty green one comes next, one step too far.
questions.strategy: When the columns do not match up, stop reading down and read the whole grid as one long line.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A grid where diamonds and stars take turns while the colors repeat in threes. One piece is missing.

choices.label: a yellow star with flat stripes
a yellow diamond with flat stripes

questions.explanation: Two patterns run at the same time. Diamond and star take turns, and the colors repeat every three pieces, so the two never line up. Counting along, the hole is a star, and its color is striped yellow. The striped yellow diamond gets the color right but the shape wrong.
questions.strategy: Track one pattern all the way along first, then go back and track the other.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: Pentagons taking turns: filled blue, then empty green. The first pentagon on the bottom row is missing.

questions.explanation: Filled blue and empty green take turns right through the grid, so the piece after the last empty green one is a filled blue pentagon. The hole also sits under a filled blue pentagon, which agrees. The empty blue pentagon has the right color but the wrong filling.
questions.strategy: A hole at the start of a row is no harder. Carry on from the end of the row above.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid where every piece in a row is the same shape, the same color and pointing the same way. One piece in the top row is missing.

questions.explanation: Every piece in a row matches, and the top row is gray arrows pointing right. The gray arrow pointing down is the right shape and color but it has been turned, and nothing else in the row is turned.
questions.strategy: Check three things in a row item: shape, color and which way it faces.

questions.prompt: Which piece belongs in the empty space?

figure.alt: Two rows of yellow shapes repeating in the same order. One shape is missing.

choices.label: a yellow crescent facing the other way

questions.explanation: The four shapes repeat in order, so each column always holds the same shape. The crescent sits above the hole, so a crescent goes in the hole. The crescent facing the other way is turned round, and nothing else in this grid is turned.
questions.strategy: In a repeating grid, look straight up. The column tells you the shape.

questions.prompt: Which piece belongs in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid of leaning quadrilaterals. Each column has its own color and its own filling. One piece is missing.

choices.label: a green shape with upright stripes
a blue shape with upright stripes
a green shape with flat stripes
a green trapezoid with upright stripes

questions.explanation: The color and the filling both belong to the column, and the second column is green with upright stripes. The green shape with flat stripes is very close, but its stripes lie the wrong way.
questions.strategy: When two answers look almost the same, find the one detail that separates them and check it carefully.

questions.prompt: Which piece belongs in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid of green trapezoids. They point up and down in a checkerboard. One is missing.

choices.label: a green trapezoid with its wide edge on top
a green trapezoid with its wide edge at the bottom
a green trapezoid turned on its side
a yellow trapezoid with its wide edge on top

questions.explanation: The color never changes, so the whole pattern is in the way the trapezoids face. They flip over every step across and every step down, and all four neighbors of the hole point the same way, so the hole points the other way. The one turned on its side never appears anywhere in the grid.
questions.strategy: When every piece is the same color, the answer is hiding in the way the pieces face.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A grid of blue right-angled triangles that turn a little further at every step. The last one is missing.

choices.label: a blue right-angled triangle with its square corner at the top right
a blue right-angled triangle turned an eighth less
a blue right-angled triangle turned an eighth further
a blue right-angled triangle turned the other way
a yellow right-angled triangle with its square corner at the top right

questions.explanation: Every step to the right turns the triangle an eighth of a turn, and the bottom row runs a half turn, then five eighths, so the hole is three quarters of a turn. The one turned an eighth less is simply the piece to the left of the hole copied over.
questions.strategy: Work out the size of one turn, then add it on. Do not try to picture the whole spin at once.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A grid of six-pointed stars. Each row is one color and filled and empty stars take turns along every row. One star is missing.

questions.explanation: The row gives the color, which is green, and filled and empty take turns, so after an empty star comes a filled one. The striped green star is the closest trap: nothing in this grid is striped, only filled or empty.
questions.strategy: Make a short list of the fillings that actually appear. Anything else is a trap.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: Twelve empty gray squares, each holding a small black dot. The dot sits where its own square sits in the grid. One square is missing.

choices.label: an empty gray square with a black dot just right of center
an empty gray square with a black dot high and just right of center
an empty gray square with a black dot just left of center
an empty gray square with a black dot near the right edge
an empty blue square with a black dot just right of center

questions.explanation: Each square is a little map of the whole grid, and the dot marks that square's own spot. The hole is in the middle row and the third column, so the dot sits halfway down and a bit right of center. The dot near the right edge belongs to the fourth column, one place too far over.
questions.strategy: Point at the hole, then point at the same place inside the answer. They should match.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A grid where the shape comes from the column, the color comes from the row, and the number grows by one in every direction. The last box is missing.

questions.explanation: Three rules run at once: the column gives the cross, the row gives yellow, and the count climbs by one across and down, so the hole holds five. Each wrong answer keeps two rules and breaks exactly one. Four crosses breaks only the counting rule.
questions.strategy: With three rules, count them on your fingers and test every answer against all three.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: Sixteen ovals repeating in threes: filled blue, striped yellow, empty green. The rows are four wide, so the pattern shifts along. One oval is missing.

choices.label: a striped yellow oval standing upright

questions.explanation: Three ovals repeat but the rows hold four, so nothing lines up in the columns and reading down will mislead you. Read the whole grid as one long line and the oval before the hole is filled blue, so the hole is striped yellow. The filled yellow oval has the color right and the filling wrong.
questions.strategy: If the columns do not repeat, the pattern is a line, not a grid. Read it end to end.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: Black four-pointed stars and black rings taking turns in two rows. One piece is missing.

questions.explanation: Star and ring take turns all the way through, and the piece before the hole is a star, so the hole is a ring. The solid black circle looks similar but a ring has a hole in the middle and the circle does not.
questions.strategy: Look for the one feature that separates two lookalike answers, then check it in the grid.

questions.prompt: Which piece fits in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid of green shapes where every column holds the same shape. One shape is missing.

choices.label: a green cross with wider arms
a green plus tilted like an X

questions.explanation: Each column keeps one shape all the way down, and the third column is the plus. The tilted plus is the same shape turned into an X, and nothing in this grid is tilted.
questions.strategy: Cover the rest of the grid with your hand and look only at the column the hole is in.

questions.prompt: Which piece belongs in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid of squares where each row has its own color and its own filling. One square is missing.

choices.label: a yellow square with a criss cross pattern

questions.explanation: Color and filling both come from the row, and the third row is yellow with dots. The yellow square with a criss cross is the near miss: the color is right but that filling appears nowhere in the grid.
questions.strategy: Before choosing, list the fillings that really appear in the grid. Reject any answer that invents a new one.

questions.prompt: Which piece belongs in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid of arrows. Each column has its own color and points its own way. One arrow is missing.

questions.explanation: Color and direction travel together down each column, and the last column is gray pointing up. The gray arrow pointing down is the same color turned the opposite way, which is the easiest mistake to make.
questions.strategy: Direction is easy to flip by accident. Trace the arrow above the hole with your finger before you answer.

questions.prompt: Which piece belongs in the empty space?

figure.alt: A grid of blue hexagons. Filled ones and dotted ones sit in a checkerboard. One hexagon is missing.

choices.label: a blue hexagon with a criss cross pattern

questions.explanation: Every hexagon is blue, so the color tells you nothing and the whole pattern lives in the filling. Filled and dotted alternate in both directions, and all of the hole's neighbors are filled, so the hole is dotted. The criss cross filling never appears in the grid at all.
questions.strategy: When one attribute never changes, ignore it completely and hunt for the one that does.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A grid of blue arrows. Going right they turn backwards an eighth of a turn each time, and going down they turn forwards a quarter. The last arrow is missing.

choices.label: a blue arrow pointing up and to the left
a blue arrow pointing down and to the left

questions.explanation: Going right the arrows turn anticlockwise by an eighth, so the bottom row runs up, then up and left, then left. The arrow pointing up is what you get by turning the wrong way, and it is the trap here.
questions.strategy: Decide which way the turn goes before you start, and say it out loud: clockwise or anticlockwise.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A grid of kites. Each row is one color, and filled and striped kites take turns along every row. One kite is missing.

choices.label: a gray kite with upright stripes
a gray kite with flat stripes

questions.explanation: The bottom row is gray, and filled and striped take turns, so after a striped kite comes a filled one. The gray kite with flat stripes is the near miss, because its stripes run the wrong way and it should not be striped at all.
questions.strategy: Check the filling of the piece immediately before the hole, not just the color of the row.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A grid of green stars. The number grows by one going across and by one going down. One box is missing.

questions.explanation: The count is the row number plus the column number, so along the bottom row it runs three, four, five, six and the hole holds five. Four is the box to the left of the hole, which is the most common slip. Nothing else about the stars changes.
questions.strategy: Say the row out loud as a counting sequence. Your ear catches a missing number faster than your eye.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A grid where the shapes repeat every three pieces and the colors repeat every four, so the two patterns slide past each other. One piece is missing.

questions.explanation: Two patterns run at different speeds. The shapes go triangle, square, circle over and over, and the colors go blue, green, yellow, gray over and over, so they only line up every twelve pieces. Counting along the line, the hole is the triangle position and the green position, so it is an empty green triangle. The empty green square keeps the color and loses the shape.
questions.strategy: Count the shape pattern along the whole line first. Then start again and count the color pattern.

questions.prompt: Which piece completes the pattern?

figure.alt: A grid of trapezoids. They turn an eighth further at every step to the right, and going down they shrink and change color. One is missing.

choices.label: a small yellow trapezoid turned an eighth
a small yellow trapezoid turned a quarter
a medium yellow trapezoid turned an eighth
a small green trapezoid turned an eighth
a small yellow leaning quadrilateral turned an eighth

questions.explanation: Three rules run together: the turn comes from the column, and the size and the color both come from the row. The hole is in the middle column and the bottom row, so it is turned an eighth, small and yellow. Each wrong answer obeys two of the three rules and breaks one, and the medium yellow one breaks only the size.
questions.strategy: Write the three rules down as column rule, row size, row color. Then test each answer against all three.
